practice.scenario: You need an investor update deck covering last quarter: revenue up 40%, two enterprise customers signed, churn slightly worse, and a hiring ask.
practice.task: Choose the prompt most likely to produce a deck you can present without rebuilding it.

options.text: "Create a professional investor update presentation for our startup's Q3 results."

"8-card investor update. Card 1: headline, revenue up 40% QoQ. Cards 2 to 3: the two enterprise logos signed and what they unlock. Card 4: churn rose from 3% to 4%, with the cause and the fix. Cards 5 to 6: hiring ask, two engineers, with the reasoning. Card 7: risks. Card 8: what we need from you. Direct tone, numbers in headlines, no filler."
"Make the best possible investor deck. Use your judgment on structure and make it visually stunning."

practice.revealLabel: See why the second prompt wins
practice.feedback: The second prompt wins because it supplies the two things Gamma cannot infer: the structure (how many cards and what goes on each) and the specifics (40%, 3% to 4%, two engineers). Given only a topic, the model fills space with generic business language, which is where the "AI deck" look comes from. Notice it also carries the uncomfortable number. A deck that hides worsening churn does not survive the first question, and telling the tool to include it is how you keep the argument honest. The vague prompts produce something that looks finished and says nothing.

body.html:
Gamma's output quality tracks the specificity of your prompt almost linearly. Give it a topic and you get filler with nice typography. Give it a structure and real numbers and you get a draft worth editing.

The pattern that works: state the number of cards, say what belongs on each, include your actual figures, and set a tone. It feels like more work than typing a sentence, and it is, but it replaces the twenty minutes you would otherwise spend rewriting generic content.

Gamma uses cards that grow to fit their content rather than fixed-size slides. Text does not get squashed to fit a template, which removes the most common cause of ugly decks.

There is also a document mode that produces long-form scrollable content instead of a card-by-card deck, which suits memos, reports, and proposals. Choosing the wrong mode is a common early mistake: if the output is meant to be read rather than presented, document mode is the better container.

The free plan comes with 400 one-time AI credits. A full deck generation costs roughly 40, so you get about 8 to 10 generated decks. Free credits do not refresh, though referrals add more, and paid plans provide a refreshing monthly allowance.

The practical consequence: do not use generation as a thinking tool. Work out your structure first, then generate once against a detailed prompt, then edit by hand. Regenerating repeatedly to "see what it comes up with" is how people burn 400 credits in an afternoon and end up with a deck no better than their second attempt.

PDF, PPTX, and PNG export are available across plans. They are not equally reliable.

Because Gamma's native format is a flexible web layout, PPTX export often shifts layouts and substitutes fonts, and complex cards can arrive in PowerPoint as flattened, non-editable images. PDF preserves the design most faithfully and is the safer choice for sharing and printing.

If someone downstream genuinely needs to edit in PowerPoint, plan for that from the start and keep cards simple, or accept that you will be doing cleanup on the other side.

faq.q: How many free credits does Gamma give you?
faq.a: The free plan includes 400 one-time AI credits. A full presentation generation costs roughly 40, so that is around 8 to 10 generated decks. Free credits do not refresh, though referrals earn more and paid plans include a refreshing monthly allowance.

faq.q: What is the difference between cards and slides in Gamma?
faq.a: Cards resize to fit their content instead of forcing content into a fixed slide. That removes the usual problem of text being squeezed to fit a template. Gamma also offers a document mode for long-form scrollable content like memos and reports.

faq.q: Can you export Gamma to PowerPoint?
faq.a: Yes, PPTX export is available on all plans, but it is the least reliable format. Layouts often shift, fonts get substituted, and complex cards can arrive as flattened images that cannot be edited. PDF preserves the original design most faithfully.

faq.q: How do I get a better deck out of Gamma?
faq.a: Prompt the structure rather than the topic. Say how many cards you want, what belongs on each, include your real numbers, and set a tone. A topic-only prompt produces generic filler, which is where the recognisable AI-deck look comes from.

faq.q: Is Gamma good for documents as well as presentations?
faq.a: Yes. Document mode produces long-form scrollable content rather than cards, which suits memos, reports, and proposals better than a presentation format does.
